items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: His name wa s Earl Norman and his wife's name was Stella. I really felt at home with these people who were more like a brother and sister to me than my landlord and landlady.

ctx.x: For some weeks I roomed with a woman named Mrs Fips on St.Nicholas Avenue. at the corner of 153rd street. Coleman Hawkins lived not far from me on 153rd street and also a bass player named John Brown. Whenever Illinois Jacquet came to New York, he stayed at this place and Mrs Fips always had a room reserved for him. Her son's name was Bobby and he knew many of the younger musicians and people in show business. It was Bobby who introduced me to Babs(Lee Brown) Gonzales.

One day, the landlord of the house where I had lived with Beezie on 154th street came to see me and told me that he had a room to rent and I jumped at the opportunity quicker than it takes to say'Jack Rabbit', because this fellow and I had many things in common which I had discovered when I lived in his house before Beezie and I separated. His name wa s Earl Norman and his wife's name was Stella. I really felt at home with these people who were more like a brother and sister to me than my landlord and landlady.

Sy Oliver had left the orchestra of Tommy Dorsey for whom he had been the arranger after he had split from Jimmie Lunceford and it must have been around the middle of November, 1946, that I heard through the grapevine that Sy was forming an orchestra and would be auditioning musicians at a rehearsal studio on Broadway.
